reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: A central abdominal wall defect at the umbilicus in which abdominal contents herniate into a sac formed by peritoneum and amniotic membrane, with the cord inserting onto the sac
The covering sac distinguishes it from gastroschisis and offers some protection, but it can rupture during delivery or handling
Strongly associated with other anomalies, including chromosomal disorders, cardiac defects, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, so a thorough workup is essential
Large or giant defects may contain the liver, complicating reduction and closure and raising the risk of respiratory compromise
Initial management protects the sac, keeps it moist and covered, maintains temperature and fluids, and decompresses the stomach
Small defects can often be closed primarily, whereas giant omphaloceles may be managed with staged reduction or a delayed approach allowing the sac to epithelialise
Associated pulmonary hypoplasia and hypoglycaemia (in Beckwith-Wiedemann) must be anticipated and monitored
Antenatal detection allows delivery planning, genetic counselling, and fetal echocardiography
reference.pathophysiology: Omphalocele results from failure of the midgut to return fully to the abdominal cavity and complete the normal closure of the abdominal wall at the umbilical ring during early gestation. The herniated viscera remain covered by a membranous sac of peritoneum and amnion with Wharton's jelly between them. Because the defect reflects a broader disturbance of ventral body wall folding, it is frequently accompanied by chromosomal, cardiac, and syndromic abnormalities, and large defects are associated with a small, underdeveloped abdominal cavity and pulmonary hypoplasia.
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound and karyotyping given the high rate of chromosomal anomalies
Fetal and postnatal echocardiography to detect cardiac defects
Blood glucose monitoring, particularly if Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is suspected
Assessment of respiratory status for possible pulmonary hypoplasia in giant defects
Renal and cranial imaging as part of anomaly screening
redFlags: Rupture of the sac exposing viscera, converting it to an emergency similar to gastroschisis with major fluid and heat loss
Respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia or from raised intra-abdominal pressure after reduction
Severe hypoglycaemia in the context of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Haemodynamic instability from a major associated cardiac anomaly
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is driven largely by associated anomalies rather than the defect itself; isolated small omphaloceles do well, whereas giant defects and those with chromosomal, cardiac, or pulmonary problems carry higher morbidity and mortality. Staged management of giant lesions can yield good long-term results.
pitfalls: Allowing the sac to dry out or become damaged through poor handling
Failing to search for and manage associated cardiac and chromosomal anomalies
Forcing rapid reduction of a giant defect and precipitating abdominal compartment syndrome or respiratory failure
Overlooking hypoglycaemia in infants with features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Immediate neonatal stabilisation: protect the sac and keep it moist and covered, maintain temperature and fluids, and decompress the stomach with a nasogastric tube
Surgical closure with primary repair for small defects, and staged reduction with a silo or delayed epithelialisation (paint and wait) for giant defects
Thorough screening for associated anomalies, including chromosomal disorders, cardiac defects on echocardiography and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Monitor for and treat hypoglycaemia, particularly where Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is suspected
Respiratory support for pulmonary hypoplasia and the effects of raised intra-abdominal pressure in giant defects
Nutritional support including parenteral nutrition until enteral feeding is established
Multidisciplinary neonatal, paediatric surgical, cardiology and clinical genetics care
Genetic counselling and karyotyping given the high rate of chromosomal and syndromic association
